en: He cried out as they went.
“Do not die, my warrior, my lord!”
Your renowned sister-in-law Kanykei
Grew worn as she went.
The well-fed lamb, that sweet head,
Semetey was beneath her arm.
She fed him meat from their provisions.
The milk poured into the leather flask,
To her only child, whom she counted on,
Semetey, she gave to suck.
The cooked meat upon the bones
She fed to Chyiyrdy.
Finding no rest by day,
Getting no sleep by night,
Never stopping each day,
Taking no time from the daylight,
Traveling day and night,
Covering ground without sparing the horses,
Putting much road behind them,
At Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi—
At Kul-Tokoi they now arrived and camped.
They called it Father Kul-Tokoi.
Countless saints had spread their hands there;
It was a place where light had poured down.
Blessed place, its apples ripened and fell to compost.
Pure saints and holy elders
Had spent the night there.
Walnuts fell from the trees.
To the woman crying out in anguish,
That Kul-Tokoi where she stood
Appeared like true paradise.
The cuckoo spoke from the plane tree,
The owl called upon its mountain.
There, snowcocks cried from the hills,
From the lower slopes, chukars and birds swooped down.
Nightingales sang from this forest,
Parrots spoke from the willows.
There were living souls and animals;
In Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi
Everything the Creator made was there.
If you looked just before you,
There were plane trees the size of houses.
Not a cup-sized patch of the plane tree was intact;
Upon every branch there was a nest.
If she looked at one branch,
Kites that flew with drooping wings had nested.
If she looked at another branch,
Blue-mottled-necked jackdaws had nested.
If she looked at another branch,
Rooks with bulging throats had nested.
If she looked toward the lower end,
The fork-tailed one had nested there.
When she looked then,
Every kind of living creature had bred there.
Its birds had hatched in the birches;
When your fierce woman looked,
They stood preparing to fly.
Its birds had hatched in the poplars;
They stood eager to take wing.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi—
When she went into its midst,
Its leaves were like leather.
A saint had lain there;
Its black worms were as big as thumbs.
Kanykei reached the great poplar,
Removed the saddles, leaving the horses bare.
That noble leopard Bakai—
With the great hobbles he had given as a gift,
She hobbled those winged steeds above the hooves.
The white lead rope tied with a loop-knot
She fastened again, drawing them close.
There, in breezy Ken-Ozon,
Those accomplished winged coursers
She entrusted to the great poplar.
The white saddles made by your noble Alake
They each laid beneath their heads.
With their heads toward the qibla,
They lay down to sleep their fill,
Resting their bodies upon their sides,
Sleeping propped upon an elbow,
Taking a quiet nap.
Beseeching her Allah,
The battle-axe left by noble Manas,
Your lion-like sister-in-law Kanykei
Held in her right hand.
After she had dozed a while,
Kanykei woke from sleep with a start.
Alas, that poor handmaid, like a rooster,
Turned onto her right side.
The pain in her chafed feet had eased.
Your mother who traveled the road
Opened her eyes, small as dough pellets.
When she rose from sleep, awake,
Those winged steeds, their flesh restored,
Were tossing wildly,
Chewing their bits and straining.
Laying back their right ears,
The coursers snorted,
The crust of the black earth
They flung up toward the sky.
When your sister-in-law rose from sleep,
Stars trembled in the heavens,
One by one toward the qibla.
Stars streaked from the sky,
Racing toward the qibla.
Dawn split open and swelled,
The rear of dawn loomed broad.
Dawn advanced clear and bright,
And light had entered the earth.
Turning, Kanykei the courser,
The gray belt left by her khan Manas
Placed snugly about her neck.
The generous one who had gone to the other world—
She beseeched his spirit.
That Kanykei, built like a warrior,
Toward the plane tree where the horses were tied
Walked slowly up.
Then the black steel bits
She took from each horse's mouth.
Dark sedge and fine grass
She let them graze along the ridges.
From the bubbling spring
She let them quench their thirst.
The coursers, like young foals,
She let roll upon the sandy ground.
Your wretched sister-in-law Kanykei—
Allah's sun grew clouded in the sky.
Unable to remain in that forest,
Sixty worries came at once into her head.
Tears poured from her eyes,
Her poor heart was torn.
“If the day is moon-dark,
What will the night be like?
If the Kokand people come hunting here
And come upon this fierce woman,
What will become of her day?
If he comes upon me,
Will they together bring about my end?
Semetey, whom I saw after his father's death—
Will the unbelievers and their high official carry him away?
‘The woman who threw a people into turmoil—
Here is that shameless, fierce woman!’ they will say.
Will they offer me up as a sacrifice?
My orphan left by my companion,
‘We have ruined them and taken booty,’ they will say.
Will they make him a slave for life?
Will they bring torment upon his head?
My only child who came from my womb,
My little one left by my khan—
Will they inflict the full measure of suffering?
Andijan, Kokand and Margilan—
Will they take my orphan as booty?
Parted from her orphan through rash wandering,
Will God strike down the widow?
My precious mother,
Can a restless person remain still?
Your orphan unable to escape,
Will God strike down the widow?
We fled impetuously toward Bukhara;
Are we never to reach Bukhara?!”
So saying, Kanykei
Set her provisions ready at her side.
The arms for entering a firefight
She fastened snugly about her waist.
Hastily she recited her prayers
And saddled the winged steeds.
Your leopard-like sister-in-law could not stay,
Fearing for her orphan.
Unable to bear lying in the forest,
Your wretched sister-in-law gathered herself,
Finding no room upon the earth.
The forest where she lay was a dense thicket.
Unable to remain, begging and weeping,
Her heart seethed with grief.
That widow left by Manas,
Her thoughts deeply troubled,
The poor woman took as her support
That child left by the warrior.
Parted from her lion,
Your warrior sister-in-law Kanykei
Turned toward the city of Bukhara.
Your renowned sister-in-law Kanykei,
That poor woman with a warrior's build,
When she had met Manas,
Had joined together what was torn,
Had gathered what was scattered.
She who had been headstrong as a maiden,
To Manas, blessed by Khyzyr,
She had once come like the Night of Power.
When she met him, she made him a khan.
Your tiger-khan, the fierce-maned wolf—
She set all around him in order.
She had him called Lord Manas,
Made the warrior khan over all around,
And put his four kinds of livestock in order.
Bringing things about through her thought,
All his chests
She filled with yellow gold and property.
She set his heart greatly at ease.
The fierce wolf Manas, the leopard,
She made khan wherever he reached.
Planting and setting out, she made gardens;
Building and kneading clay, she made houses.
She set all his equipment in order.
At thirty-two years old,
Parted from the king,
Kanykei fled in mourning.
Then Semetey fled and wandered.
Your courageous leopard-like sister-in-law,
Your saint left by bloodthirsty Manas,
Showed that she was a hero.
That Duldul among dark horses,
That Chyiyrdy who had grown old,
Showed that she was a hero.
The precious aged mother
She mounted upon Akborchuk.
Then your saintly sister-in-law Kanykei
Lashed her whip this way and that,
Spurring to right and left,
Traveling the long road without sparing herself,
Covering ground without sparing the horse.
As she spurred, the saddle-flaps swayed;
The winged steed's sweat streamed down,
Now splashing at the stirrups.
Through the desert veiled in haze,
Across rough and knobbly passes,
Along the twisting road,
Along the winding waters,
Along the road to Bukhara,
How could your sister-in-law spare herself?
Having traveled a great distance,
Her father Temir Khan's broad Ak-Chii—
She approached its boundary then.
When she crossed that boundary,
Her heart sank and was torn.
When she saw the land she knew,
Your fierce, wolf-maned sister-in-law—
Then tears poured from her eyes.
Those dear eyes like currants,
When she saw the dear land,
Shed tears a whip's length long.
Those dear eyes like a quail's,
When she saw that land,
Shed separate streams of tears:
“Oh, my precious mother,
My sacred mother, whom I counted on!
You bore a lion among sons,
You bore a hero among daughters,
My golden-wombed mother.
Amir-Temir, Kuroogon—
He was my grandfather.
Once, saying, ‘I shall bring torment to Beijing,
The only daughter of Khan Alooko in Beijing,
That beauty Medirese,
I shall take as my wife,’
He gathered troops from the sons of the Turks,
